title: 〜よう — casual "let's"
pattern: 〜よう・〜おう（{行|い}こう・{食|た}べよう）
explanation: The plain volitional form is the casual version of 〜ましょう: it means "let's …", and it's what partners say to each other. る-verbs swap る for よう (たべる → たべよう); う-verbs change their last u-sound to o and add う (いく → いこう, のむ → のもう); する → しよう and くる → こよう. Add か for a softer "shall we …?" (〜ようか), and use 〜ようとおもう for "I'm thinking of …". With people you don't know well, stay with 〜ましょう.

title: 〜より・〜のほうが — comparing two things
explanation: Use より for "than". AよりBのほうが + adjective means "B is more … than A": いぬよりねこのほうがすき, "I like cats more than dogs". You can also start with the winner: BはAより〜. To ask which of two, say AとBと、どちらが〜ですか (polite) or AとB、どっちが〜？ (casual), and answer with 〜のほうが. The adjective itself never changes; for "the most" out of three or more, use いちばん instead.

title: 〜ないでください — "please don't"
explanation: To ask someone not to do something, take the plain negative (ない form) and add でください: たべない → たべないでください, "please don't eat it". title: 〜んです — explaining and asking why
explanation: Adding んです to a plain-form sentence turns it into an explanation, like "the thing is …". Use it to explain a situation (あたまがいたいんです, "I've got a headache") or to ask about something you've noticed (どうしたんですか, "what's wrong?"). Nouns and な-adjectives take な first: やすみなんです. title: なにか・なにも — "something", "nothing"
explanation: Add か to a question word to make "some-": なにか (something), だれか (someone), どこか (somewhere), いつか (some day). Add も and a negative verb for "no-": なにも〜ない (nothing), だれも〜ない (no one). In questions, なにか means "anything", and the words work the same in polite and casual speech: なにかのみますか to a guest, なにかのむ？ to your partner. Particles like に and と stay in front of も: どこにもいかない, "I'm not going anywhere".

title: 〜とき — "when …"
explanation: とき means "when" or "at the time". Put a plain verb or い-adjective right before it (さむいとき), な-adjectives keep な (ひまなとき), and nouns take の (こどものとき). Use the past before とき when that action is already done at the time: にほんにいったとき, "when we went to Japan", or つかれたとき, "when I get tired". The part before とき stays plain even in polite speech; only the end of the sentence shows politeness (ひまなとき、なにをしますか). For "before" and "after", use まえに and あとで (coming soon), and for "if / once (something happens)", 〜たら comes later.

title: 〜くて・〜で — joining descriptions
explanation: To join two descriptions ("cheap and tasty"), put the first one in its て-form. い-adjectives swap い for くて: やすい → やすくて, and いい becomes よくて. な-adjectives and nouns add で: しずかできれい ("quiet and pretty"), アメリカじんで ("American, and …"). Only the last word shows the tense or politeness, so 〜くて〜です is polite and 〜くて〜かった is past. title: 〜ほん・〜まい — counters for things
explanation: Japanese counts most things with a counter word after the number. The common ones: 〜ほん for long, thin things and bottles; 〜まい for flat things like paper, tickets and shirts; 〜はい for cups and glasses; 〜こ for small items; 〜ひき for small animals; 〜さつ for books; and 〜かい for times. Some numbers change sound: いっぽん, さんぼん, ろっぽん; いっぱい, さんばい; いっこ, ろっこ; いっぴき, さんびき. The number goes after the thing and its particle, just like ひとつ (ビールをにほんください), and you ask with なん + counter (なんぼん, なんまい). Counters are the same in polite and casual speech, and if one slips your mind, ひとつ, ふたつ … still works for most objects.

explanation: To talk about life experience (things you have or haven't done at some point), use the plain past た form + ことがある: すしをたべたことがある, "I've eaten sushi before". title: 〜ほうがいい — "you'd better"

explanation: To give advice, use the plain past た form + ほうがいい: はやくねたほうがいい, "you'd better go to bed early". For "you'd better not", use the plain ない form + ほうがいい: のまないほうがいい. title: 〜ので — "because" (softer)
explanation: ので means "because" or "so", like から, but it sounds softer and more considerate, so it's the natural choice for excuses and requests to people you don't know well. The reason comes first: ようじがあるので、さきにかえります, "I have something to do, so I'll head off first". Plain forms usually go before ので, and nouns and な-adjectives take な: あめなので, ひまなので. Between partners, から is more common; ので sounds a little more careful. You can also end a sentence with ので and leave the rest unsaid, as a polite explanation.

explanation: つもり means "intention": a plan you've already made up your mind about. Put the dictionary form before it for "I plan to …" (らいねんにほんにいくつもりです) and the ない form for "I don't plan to …". title: 〜って — casual quoting
explanation: って is the casual spoken form of と and という. It reports what someone said: あしたはあめだって, "they say it'll rain tomorrow". It names things: 「さくら」っていうカフェ, "a cafe called Sakura". It's everywhere in partner chat and messages, but in polite speech and writing use と and という instead.

title: 〜は — contrast, "as for X …"
explanation: Besides marking the topic, は can show contrast: "X, (unlike Y) …". にくはたべるけど、さかなはたべない (polite: にくはたべますが、さかなはたべません) means "Meat I eat, but fish I don't". It often comes in pairs like that, or alone to hint at an unspoken contrast: ビールはのまない, "beer I don't drink (other things, maybe)". は can follow other particles to contrast them (ここでは, にちようびには), and it often appears in negatives: すきではない. Remember the split: が points at new information or the answer to a question word, while は sets up the topic or a contrast.

title: 〜なければならない — "have to"
pattern: 〜なければならない・〜なきゃ
explanation: To say "have to" or "must", take the ない form, change ない to なければ, and add ならない (polite なりません): おきる → おきなければならない, "I have to get up". なければいけない means the same and is very common in speech. Between partners, the short forms 〜なきゃ and 〜なくちゃ are what you'll actually hear: あしたはやくおきなきゃ. This is a real obligation; for advice use 〜ほうがいい, for "must not" use 〜てはいけない, and "don't have to" (〜なくてもいい) comes later.

title: 〜く・〜に — how you do something
explanation: To say how something is done, turn the adjective into an adverb. い-adjectives change い to く: はやい → はやく ("early, quickly"), and いい → よく ("well"). な-adjectives add に: しずか → しずかに ("quietly"), じょうず → じょうずに ("skillfully"). The adverb goes before the verb: はやくおきる, しずかにはなす. These are the same く and に forms you used with なる, so しずかになる is "become quiet" while しずかにはなす is "talk quietly"; with して they make casual requests: はやくして！ ("hurry up!").

title: 〜ながら — "while"
explanation: ながら means "while": one person doing two things at the same time. Take the ます form, drop ます, and add ながら: ききます → ききながら, たべます → たべながら. The main action comes last, and the ながら action is the background: おんがくをききながらりょうりする, "I cook while listening to music". Both actions must be done by the same person; for two different people, use 〜ているとき instead. Only the final verb shows politeness, so it fits polite and casual sentences alike.

title: こんな・どんな — "this kind of", "what kind of"
pattern: こんな・そんな・あんな・どんな／こう・そう・ああ・どう
explanation: This set works like これ and ここ, but for kinds and ways. こんな / そんな / あんな / どんな + noun mean "this kind of / that kind of / that kind of (over there) / what kind of": どんなひと？, "what kind of person?". こう / そう / ああ / どう go with verbs for "like this / like that / how": こうかく ("write it like this"), そうおもう ("I think so"), どうやって ("how, by what means"). As before, こ- is near me, そ- is near you or what was just said, あ- is over there or something we both know, and ど- asks. They're used the same way in polite and casual speech, and together with これ and ここ they complete the こそあど table.

title: 〜ことができる — "can do"
explanation: できる means "can" or "be able to". After a noun, use が: りょうりができる, "can cook"; にほんごができる, "can speak Japanese". After a verb, use the dictionary form + ことができる: ここでカードをつかうことができますか. Like the の in のがすき, こと turns the verb into a noun, but with できる you need こと, not の, and the result sounds a little formal; in everyday talk the potential form (たべられる), which comes soon, is more common. できる also means "be ready" (ごはんできたよ！) and, for a new shop or building, "open".

title: あげる・もらう — giving and receiving
explanation: あげる means "give" when the gift goes away from you (or your side) to someone else: つまにはなをあげた, "I gave my wife flowers"; the person who receives takes に. もらう means "receive, get": the receiver is the subject, and the giver takes に or から: おっとにとけいをもらった, "I got a watch from my husband". title: Potential form — "can do"
explanation: The potential form is the everyday way to say "can". る-verbs change る to られる (たべる → たべられる; in casual speech you'll often hear たべれる), and う-verbs change their last u-sound to an e-sound and add る (のむ → のめる, いく → いける); する becomes できる and くる becomes こられる. The thing you can do often takes が instead of を (にほんごがはなせる), and the new verb works like any る-verb: はなせます, はなせない. 〜ことができる means the same but sounds more formal. The passive (a later lesson) looks like the る-verb potential, so context tells them apart.
